items.title: The science, medicine, and mythology of menstruation and menopause
items.description:
OBGYN and author Dr. Jen Gunter explains what’s actually happening inside the body during menstruation and menopause, why so much of what we’ve been told is wrong, and why that information gap has been weaponized against half the population. 
 
 This video  The science, medicine, and mythology of menstruation and menopause  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: How to make difficult decisions, according to philosophy
items.description:
Every now and then, life asks us a question with no easy answer. Which career should we pursue? Should we have children? Should we move to the coast or closer to our friends? 
 We gather information, read testimonials, and exhaustively research both options. One path seems better in some ways, the other seems better in others, and we find ourselves stuck between them. The best answer eludes us.

items.title: The rule of 20%: How to find the sweet spot for improved performance
items.description:
Talent isn’t a gift we’re born with – it’s a signal we’ve been reading completely wrong. Author Daniel Coyle breaks down the common traits shared by successful people, and why environment, not innate ability, is the variable that ties them all together. 
 
 This video  The rule of 20%: How to find the sweet spot for improved performance  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: Why mirrors flip left-to-right but not up-and-down
items.description: If you’ve ever looked in a mirror, you’ve likely noticed that everything you see is flipped. When you raise your left hand, your reflection raises their right hand. When you wink with your right eye, your reflection’s left eye winks back. And if you write a message and hold it up, you’ll see your reflection hold up the identical sign, but everything appears backward, even the individual letters themselves. items.description:

items.title: Ask Ethan: Are there really charm quarks inside the proton?
items.description: At the start of the 20th century, we were still figuring out what the structure of matter was. We knew everything was made up of atoms, and that there were negatively charged electrons within them, but the rest of the atom was a mystery. Over the course of the past 125 years, we subsequently learned that there was a small, massive, positively charged nucleus anchoring every atom. items.title: Time is a fundamentally different type of dimension than space
items.description: One of the most common questions we can ask about any two distinct locations is, “What’s the shortest distance between those two points?” By default, most of us will give the same answer that Archimedes gave more than 2,000 years ago: a straight line.
